params.question: A patient habitually chews betel quid containing areca nut (supari), tobacco, and slaked lime. Why is his oral cancer risk higher than tobacco use alone would predict?

answers.text: Slaked lime neutralises the tobacco carcinogens, so his risk is actually lower than expected.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Slaked lime does not neutralise carcinogens — it raises salivary pH, which promotes release and mucosal absorption of areca nut alkaloids, adding to the carcinogenic burden rather than reducing it.

answers.text: Areca nut (supari) is itself a Group 1 carcinogen, and combined with tobacco and lime, the effect becomes multiplicative rather than additive.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies areca nut as a Group 1 carcinogen in its own right. Combined with tobacco and slaked lime in betel quid, prolonged mucosal contact produces a multiplicative carcinogenic effect, driving field cancerisation across the oral mucosa.

answers.text: Smokeless tobacco products are metabolically inert until swallowed, so chewing alone carries no independent risk.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Smokeless forms such as gutka, khaini, and mishri act directly on the oral mucosa through prolonged contact — swallowing is not required for carcinogen exposure.

answers.text: Alcohol in the betel quid mixture is the only active carcinogen; the other components are flavouring agents.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Betel quid need not contain alcohol at all. Tobacco, areca nut, and lime each contribute independently to carcinogenesis; alcohol, when co-used separately, adds its own effect via acetaldehyde generation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the mechanism: areca nut is a standalone Group 1 carcinogen, and its combination with tobacco and lime multiplies oral cancer risk through field cancerisation.
Well done — you've identified why betel quid's components act synergistically rather than independently.

params.question: On examination, you find a small red, velvety patch on the floor of the mouth in one patient and a larger white patch that cannot be scraped off in another. Which patient's lesion carries the greater risk of malignancy on biopsy?

answers.text: The white patch, because leukoplakia is always malignant.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Leukoplakia is a clinical term for a white patch, not a tissue diagnosis — only 5 to 30 percent of cases show malignant transformation, and mainly when dysplasia is present.

answers.text: The red patch, because erythroplakia shows severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ in around 90 percent of biopsies.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Erythroplakia is far more dangerous than its size suggests — roughly 90 percent of biopsies reveal severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ, which is why a smaller red lesion outranks a much larger white one in clinical urgency.

answers.text: Both carry identical risk, since colour has no bearing on histology.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Colour is a clinically meaningful clue: the velvety red appearance of erythroplakia reflects thin, non-keratinised epithelium overlying a highly vascular, often severely dysplastic stroma.

answers.text: Neither — malignant risk in oral mucosa is determined purely by lesion size.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Size does not predict malignant potential here; clinical morphology (red velvety vs white, non-scrapable) is the better predictor.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the ranking: erythroplakia (~90%) outranks leukoplakia with dysplasia (up to 30%) and oral submucous fibrosis (7–13%), regardless of lesion size.
Correct — you've applied the size-versus-colour distinction that defines urgency in oral premalignant lesions.

interactions.label: A gastric biopsy shows individual cells infiltrating the stomach wall without gl

params.question: A gastric biopsy shows individual cells infiltrating the stomach wall without gland formation, with a rigid, thickened wall on imaging. Which feature would confirm this as diffuse-type rather than intestinal-type gastric carcinoma?

answers.text: Discrete gland formation following Correa's cascade from chronic gastritis to intestinal metaplasia.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Discrete gland formation following Correa's cascade is the intestinal type — the diffuse type specifically lacks gland formation.

answers.text: Signet-ring cells packed with intracytoplasmic mucin, driven by loss of E-cadherin (the CDH1 gene).

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Diffuse-type gastric carcinoma results from loss of E-cadherin, the cell-adhesion protein encoded by CDH1. Its hallmark is signet-ring cells laden with intracytoplasmic mucin, infiltrating singly rather than forming glands, producing the rigid 'leather-bottle' stomach of linitis plastica.

answers.text: A step-wise progression through atrophic gastritis and dysplasia, typically in an older patient with a better prognosis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This step-wise sequence and better prognosis describe the intestinal type, which follows Correa's cascade. The diffuse type bypasses this sequence, strikes younger patients, and carries a worse prognosis.

answers.text: Strong association with Helicobacter pylori-driven chronic atrophic gastritis as the initiating event.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. H. pylori-driven chronic atrophic gastritis initiates Correa's cascade, underlying the intestinal type. The diffuse type's defining event is E-cadherin loss causing loss of cell adhesion, independent of this cascade.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the contrast: intestinal type forms glands via Correa's cascade; diffuse type loses E-cadherin, shows signet-ring cells, and produces linitis plastica.
Correct — you've distinguished the diffuse type's defining molecular and morphological features from the intestinal type's.

interactions.label: A biopsy from a patient with ileocaecal disease shows large, caseating, confluen

params.question: A biopsy from a patient with ileocaecal disease shows large, caseating, confluent granulomas along with transverse 'girdle' ulcers encircling the bowel. Before starting any treatment, what should this finding make you do?

answers.text: Start steroids immediately for presumed Crohn disease, since granulomas confirm the diagnosis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect, and potentially dangerous. Granulomas alone do not distinguish the two diseases — their character does. Starting steroids before excluding tuberculosis can trigger disseminated disease.

answers.text: Exclude intestinal tuberculosis first, since large caseating confluent granulomas and girdle ulcers favour tuberculosis over Crohn disease.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Intestinal tuberculosis produces large, caseating, confluent granulomas and transverse girdle ulcers, unlike the small, non-caseating, scattered granulomas and longitudinal fissures of Crohn disease. A positive interferon-gamma release assay or biopsy PCR must confirm or exclude tuberculosis before any steroid is given.

answers.text: Proceed directly to surgical resection, as granulomatous ileocaecal disease is always an indication for surgery.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Granulomatous ileocaecal disease requires diagnostic clarification first — surgery is not the default next step for either tuberculosis or Crohn disease.

answers.text: Treat empirically with both anti-tuberculous therapy and steroids simultaneously to cover either diagnosis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Steroids alongside undiagnosed tuberculosis can still precipitate dissemination; the correct approach is to confirm or exclude tuberculosis first with Mantoux testing, interferon-gamma release assay, or biopsy PCR.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall: caseating confluent granulomas and girdle ulcers point to tuberculosis; non-caseating scattered granulomas and fistulae/skip lesions point to Crohn disease. Exclude TB before any steroid.
Correct — you've applied the granuloma and ulcer-pattern clues to resolve the most dangerous diagnostic fork in GI pathology.

interactions.label: Endoscopy shows a gastric ulcer with heaped, nodular margins, a dirty necrotic b

params.question: Endoscopy shows a gastric ulcer with heaped, nodular margins, a dirty necrotic base, and mucosal folds that are interrupted rather than converging at the ulcer edge. What is the correct next step?

answers.text: Reassure the patient that these are typical benign peptic ulcer features and start acid-suppression therapy alone.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These are precisely the features of a malignant ulcer — a benign peptic ulcer has a clean base with mucosal folds that radiate in and converge at the margin.

answers.text: Biopsy the ulcer, sampling both the edges and the base, because these features suggest malignancy.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Heaped, nodular margins, a dirty necrotic base, and interrupted mucosal folds are the hallmarks of a malignant gastric ulcer, in contrast to the clean base and converging folds of a benign ulcer. Every gastric ulcer should be biopsied at the edges and base to avoid missing malignancy.

answers.text: Repeat endoscopy in six weeks without biopsy to assess healing, as is standard for all gastric ulcers.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Watchful waiting without biopsy risks missing an underlying malignancy — these gross features warrant immediate biopsy.

answers.text: Diagnose Borrmann type IV linitis plastica directly from the endoscopic appearance without tissue sampling.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Linitis plastica and the Borrmann classification rest on gross and histological findings together; endoscopic appearance alone, without biopsy confirmation, is not sufficient.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the contrast: benign ulcers are clean-based with converging folds; malignant ulcers show heaped margins, a dirty base, and interrupted folds — biopsy every gastric ulcer.
Correct — you've applied the gross morphological contrast that separates a benign ulcer from a malignant one.

interactions.label: An elderly woman presents with iron-deficiency anaemia and a positive faecal occ

params.question: An elderly woman presents with iron-deficiency anaemia and a positive faecal occult blood test but no bowel symptoms, while another patient with the same underlying molecular disease presents with pencil-thin stools and obstruction. What anatomical explanation accounts for these two very different presentations of colorectal cancer?

answers.text: Right-sided cancers grow as polypoid masses in the wide right colon causing occult bleeding and anaemia, while left-sided cancers encircle the narrow left colon causing early obstruction and napkin-ring strictures.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The wide calibre of the right colon lets a polypoid, fungating right-sided cancer grow large before causing symptoms, typically presenting with occult bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia. The narrow left colon is more easily encircled, so left-sided cancers present earlier with obstruction, pencil-thin stools, and frank rectal bleeding.

answers.text: Right-sided cancers are always more aggressive histologically, which is why they present with anaemia rather than obstruction.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The difference is anatomical calibre and growth pattern, not inherent aggressiveness — right- and left-sided cancers can arise from the same molecular pathway yet present very differently because of where they grow.

answers.text: Left-sided cancers never bleed, which is why only right-sided cancers are associated with anaemia.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Left-sided cancers do bleed, often producing frank, visible rectal bleeding — it is right-sided cancers whose bleeding is typically slow and occult, causing anaemia without visible blood.

answers.text: The difference is due to diet alone, as left-sided cancers are caused by red meat intake and right-sided cancers are not.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Dietary factors contribute to colorectal cancer risk generally, but the differing presentations described here are explained by bowel calibre and growth pattern at each site, not by diet.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall: the wide right colon permits silent, occult-bleeding growth; the narrow left colon obstructs early with a napkin-ring stricture.
Correct — you've applied the anatomy-driven explanation for why identical cancers present so differently by location.
